title: The Remaining Maxims
audit_comment: THE REMAINING FIVE MAXIMS of DMO Chapter 1 (pp. 10-29), the doctrine round closing the chapter: the intelligent-adversary doctrines (the intelligence review, the weakness shielding, the strength maximization, the handling-defeat ladder with its four options), the villain self-preservation doctrines (the villain-absence rule, the bad-guys-don't-fight-fair rules), the control-magic doctrines (the AC -4 tension floor, the memorization economics, the no-magic-shops doctrine), the plan-ahead doctrines (the growing villain, the consequences ladder, the fame ledger), and the share-responsibility doctrines (the player-DM split, the goals, the personality profile).

banner.title: THE REMAINING MAXIMS - DMO Chapter 1 closed: the intelligent-adversary doctrines (act as smart as the intelligence says, shield the weaknesses, maximize the strengths, handle defeat by motivation), the villain self-preservation rules (never be there; bad guys don't fight fair), the control-magic doctrines (the AC -4 floor, the 18-hour study vs 37-minute cast, no magic shops), the plan-ahead doctrines (villains who learn, consequences, fame), and the share-responsibility doctrines (the players as the cadre, the goals, the profile).
banner.provenance: verified against printed pp. 10-29 of the uploaded DMO session capture (part 1, printed page N at OCR page N+1); the defeat ladder from p. 13, the troll and vampire audits from pp. 12-13, the memorization economics from p. 21, the item rate from p. 28; the maxim roster from p. 6 (R599) rides the chapter parent.

consts.name: dejDefeatOptionCount
consts.comment: the handling-defeat ladder: four options open to an opponent staring defeat in the face - surrender, flee, reversal, or fight (printed p. 13).

consts.name: dejEscapeGoalCount
consts.comment: the leaving-the-field doctrine: a successful flee must accomplish three things - outrun the PCs, foil their ranged attacks, and elude long-term pursuit (printed p. 14).

consts.name: dejTrollRegenDelayRounds
consts.comment: the troll regeneration delay: the creature regains no hit points until three rounds after it suffers its first wound (printed p. 12).

consts.name: dejTrollWeaponDamageBonus
consts.comment: the troll strength read: the damage bonus when a troll employs a weapon such as a two-handed sword is +8 (printed p. 13).

consts.name: dejTensionAcFloor
consts.comment: the armor-class tension floor: once characters get below an Armor Class of -4 a great deal of the tension dissipates - the heroes are virtually immune to most physical attacks (printed p. 19).

consts.name: dejBracersAc2Bonus
consts.comment: the bracers of defense AC 2 grant an effective Armor Class bonus of +8 and should be rarer than even magical plate (printed p. 19).

consts.name: dejWizardStudyHours
consts.comment: the memorization economics: a 20th-level wizard requires 18 hours of study time to memorize a full complement of spells (printed p. 21).

consts.name: dejWizardCastMinutes
consts.comment: the memorization economics, the other half: it takes the same 20th-level wizard only 37 minutes to cast every spell in memory (printed p. 21).

consts.name: dejTeleportMemorizeMinutes
consts.comment: the teleport impracticality: the 5th-level teleport spell requires 50 minutes of memorization time, making it impractical for any trip that can be made in less than an hour by other means (printed p. 21).

consts.name: dejTeleportMinorPct
consts.comment: the teleport risk, the minor accident: even when very familiar with the destination there is a 2 percent chance per use of arriving too high (printed p. 21).

consts.name: dejTeleportFatalPct
consts.comment: the teleport risk, the fatal accident: a 1 percent chance per use of teleporting low, potentially fatal (printed p. 21).

consts.name: dejPartyItemPerAdventure
consts.comment: the balancing-act item rate: following the DMG suggestion of three to six adventures between levels, a party of six characters should find only about one magical item every adventure (printed p. 28).

bools.name: dejIntelligenceDoctrine
bools.comment: maxim two, the intelligence review: an opponent has to avoid obvious mistakes, not be brilliant - even low-intelligence foes learn from experience (the man-eating tiger at Int 2-4), and average-intelligence kobolds and goblins are as smart as a typical human (printed pp. 10-11).

bools.name: dejWeaknessShielding
bools.comment: the weakness audit: against high-level PCs few allies are expendable, and discernible weaknesses (the rakshasa blessed bolt, troll fire and acid, vampire sunlight and turning, the giant slug Armor Class) must be shielded before the fight - with the prepared advantage explained to the PCs (printed pp. 11-12).

bools.name: dejStrengthMaximization
bools.comment: the strength audit: maximize the strong points - trolls in waves with fresh troops while the hurt regenerate, vampires fighting one-on-one using gaseous form and prepared pinholes, giant slugs with stoneskin and hidden approaches (printed pp. 12-14).

bools.name: dejHandlingDefeat
bools.comment: the handling-defeat doctrine: important NPCs never check morale, only rank-and-file troops; the four options ride the motivation - coerced foes fight on, magically compelled foes cannot flee, home-front defenders fall back to attack again, looters flee at the first difficulty, proud foes attempt the dramatic reversal; the surrendering foe keeps a bargaining chip (printed pp. 12-17).

bools.name: dejLeavingFieldDoctrine
bools.comment: the leaving-the-field doctrine: run somewhere the PCs cannot follow, divert with illusions or reinforcements, slow pursuit with caltrops and webs; foil ranged attacks with cover, broken bows and antimagic shell; foil tracking with faint trails, river crossings and changed forms; cover a withdrawal with wall spells and rear guards; hit-and-run attackers strike from concealment at the spellcasters and the mounted (printed pp. 14-17).

bools.name: dejReversalDoctrine
bools.comment: the reversal doctrine: exploit the opportunity unique to the situation (the bridge supports, the flammables, the avalanche), spare the treasure the opponent wants intact, hold the potent one-use weapons in reserve, and use knowledge of the PCs as a weapon (printed p. 17).

bools.name: dejVillainSelfPreservation
bools.comment: the minimizing-personal-risks doctrine: the safest villain never goes anywhere dangerous - henchmen do the dirty work; be somewhere else (project image, the magic jar in a servant's hands, posing as a bystander or prisoner), or strike where the PCs are vulnerable but absent (their castle, their friends, their business associates) (printed pp. 16-18).

bools.name: dejBadGuysDontFightFair
bools.comment: the bad-guys-don't-fight-fair doctrine: no trick is too low - innocents block the area effects, diversions force the PCs to abandon the fight, sentimental targets goad emotional decisions, and the villain never meets the heroes without an escape route and a hidden advantage (printed p. 18).

bools.name: dejControlMagicDoctrine
bools.comment: maxim three, the control-magic core: too much magic ruins play - the PCs become exterminators and the mechanics break down; too little disheartens the players; rarity keeps the wonder (a potion momentous, a holy sword no big deal when everyone owns two); protective stacking via barter and loaning must be watched (printed pp. 17-19).

bools.name: dejMagicItemUseDoctrine
bools.comment: the item-economy doctrine: intelligent opponents use their items against the PCs and expend charged items freely when faced with defeat; captured items should be nearly drained; item saves are rolled per item when a PC fails a save (protections do not extend to equipment); villains demand items for ransom; leprechauns, storms at sea and annoyed deities remove excess magic (printed pp. 19-20).

bools.name: dejMagicShopsDoctrine
bools.comment: the no-magic-shops doctrine: magic is never a commodity - supplies come from specialty shops by barter and haggling with only a reputation as guarantee; purchases are pig-in-a-poke adventures (the fake or damaged cube of force, the rival's favor-laden loan, the dragon learning of the search); the Encyclopedia Magica values set relative worth only (printed pp. 20-21).

bools.name: dejMagicLimitationDoctrine
bools.comment: the magic-is-unlike-technology doctrine: most spells do one thing and one thing only (magic missile harms nothing inanimate, knock opens no portcullis); players with modern minds must not be allowed to treat spells as adaptable tools (printed p. 21).

bools.name: dejPlanAheadDoctrine
bools.comment: maxim six, the plan-ahead doctrine: prepare the campaign for high-level play during low-level play, neither too late nor too soon; create villains who learn - the growing villain with ambitions achieved over play, built on the six background pillars: source of power, objectives, motives, personality, history, allies (printed pp. 24-25).

bools.name: dejConsequencesDoctrine
bools.comment: the consequences doctrine: every adventure has aftereffects - someone is left behind to pick up the hoard, word spreads by boasting or witnesses, and someone always cares (helped or hurt); the charmed servant of the slain dragon is the worked example; simple incidents can hide layer upon layer (printed pp. 25-27).

bools.name: dejFameInfamyDoctrine
bools.comment: the fame-and-infamy ledger: track the PCs' reputation - exaggerated accounts of early exploits, blowhards who did know them way back when; broken word blocks later land grants and knighthoods (printed p. 27).

bools.name: dejBalancingActDoctrine
bools.comment: the balancing-act doctrine: build the balanced campaign, do not fix a runaway one - set the XP rate per DMG Chapter Eight, place the magic in advance behind appropriate risks (never the holy avenger for one orc), and take the excess out of circulation; the fair rate: one permanent or rechargeable item per two or three levels plus one or two consumables per two levels (printed p. 28).

bools.name: dejShareResponsibilityDoctrine
bools.comment: maxim seven, the share-responsibility doctrine: the players are the cadre of helpers - they detail unexplored areas, histories and NPC actions; the DM garners their interests and weaves several threads at once (the artifact example); long-term character goals beyond wealth and XP; the allies-and-enemies ledger with its favors; and the personality profile beyond the record sheet (occupation, appearance, quirks, tastes, residence, history, friends, enemies, goals) (printed pp. 27-29).
